summary: Cast-iron inner range light on the South Pier at Grand Haven, Michigan, first lit in 1905; the pier range it belongs to has been lit since 1871.

lens.note: Sources disagree: NPS and USLHS give the original optic as sixth order and the present one as 250 mm; Lighthouse Friends gives a fourth-order lens in the cylindrical tower and says the bluff lens is on display in the Train Depot Museum, Grand Haven.

structures.note: Inner tower; 51 ft tall (NPS), 52 ft steel (Conservancy). Moved about 600 ft shoreward in 1906-07 according to Lighthouse Friends and the Conservancy; the NPS inventory says not moved.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends' note for the whole Grand Haven page). The NPS inventory (archived 2007) and the USLHS record both mark the station open to the public; neither names a tower that can be climbed.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (aid); City of Grand Haven (owner, deed December 2012)

events.note: Pier (pierhead) light established on the South Pier; the station is dated 1871 by the Lighthouse Society
Steam siren in a fog-signal house under the pierhead light, operating from December 1875
Light and fog signal moved lakeward as the pier was extended (also 1885)
Gale of 9 Dec 1886 forced the pier beacon twelve feet backward (the structure of its day, not the present tower)
Tubular lantern light established to range with the pier light (30 Nov 1889)
Front range light moved 278 feet nearer the outer end of the south pier (6 July 1894)
Pierhead light moved 511 feet toward the outer end (4 May 1895); front range light discontinued
Cast-iron conical tower built near the outer end of the South Pier (the Conservancy says 52-foot steel)
Inner tower first lit; the Fresnel lens moved from the bluff tower on 12 January 1905
Temporary red light set up shoreward of the pierhead tower to form a range (28 Apr 1906)
Tower moved about 600 feet shoreward to its present location (Conservancy: 1907; LF: over the year after April 1906; NPS: not moved)
25 January 1916: keeper Joseph Kilgore rescued two Coast Guard men caught by the ice
Rear light changed from white to red; front light from red to white (15 May 1917)
Grand Haven Pierhead Range Rear change of illuminant (index entry)
14 Sept 1961: Coast Guard crewman David E. Sparks went into the water after a man washed off the pier; the rescue failed, and Sparks held a life ring until Coast Guard men reached him
Automated (NPS); Michael F. Wickman is the roster's principal keeper from 1969
Coast Guard deemed the pierhead lights excess and offered them for transfer
City of Grand Haven given a deed to the two pierhead lights (December 2012)

corrections.why: NPS (first lit 1905) and USLHS (tower established 1905) date the present inner tower to 1905. No source read gives 1881 for this tower; the pier light existed from 1871 (USLHS place record).
The 1906-07 change moved the existing cylindrical tower about 600 ft shoreward (LF, Conservancy); it was not a new tower. NPS says not moved; see notes.
NPS (archived 2007) gives Date Deactivated: N/A and the light operational; USLHS lists the aid as active.

current: Grand Marais Harbor of Refuge Inner
corrections.why: Both names come from the record's Rowlett Upper Peninsula entries (keys miwu:copper-harbor-range-rear, miwu:grand-marais-harbor-of-refuge-inner). Copper Harbor and the Grand Marais harbor of refuge are not on this pier. Not checked against the Upper Peninsula pages here.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1881 (Wikidata, Rowlett) cannot be the present tower: the NPS and USLHS date it to 1905, and the Conservancy describes the 1904-05 tower. The pier light itself dates from 1871 (USLHS), so the 1881 entry is probably the pier light of that period. Treated as a record error and proposed for correction.

LF and the Conservancy say the cylindrical tower was moved about 600 ft shoreward in 1906-07 (Conservancy: 1907). The NPS inventory answers NO to 'Has tower been moved?' Not resolved; the story reports both.

The Conservancy history puts the seawall's loss on 6 December 1852 and the collapse of the tower and cottage on 17 December. Lighthouse Friends puts the wall's collapse on the night of 17 December, the dwelling wall early the next morning, and the tower later that day. The story gives both accounts.

The NPS inventory and Cyberlights both give 1839 as the station's establishment year, and Cyberlights gives it for the inner light's original build. The Conservancy and Lighthouse Friends date the first light on the beach to 1839. No source read gives 1839 for the present inner tower (1904-05), so the story uses 1839 only for the first light.

notes_for_editor: 1) Which tower: the inner light is the cylindrical cast-iron tower first lit 1905 (NPS, USLHS). Record's 1881 and 1898 entries and its 1865 'Tower 1' have no source read for this tower; corrections proposed. 2) The record's other_names include 'Copper Harbor Range Rear' and 'Grand Marais Harbor of Refuge Inner' (Rowlett Upper Peninsula entries). Propose removal. 3) Tower move 1906-07 (LF, Conservancy) vs NPS 'not moved'. Unresolved. The USCG Historian's Grand Haven Front Light article (search snippet: 1905 rear light moved to the inner end of the pier) could not be read (live site blocked; not cited). 4) Lens: NPS and USLHS give sixth-order original optic and a 250 mm present optic; LF gives a fourth-order lens in the cylindrical tower and says the bluff lens (1854 Henry-Lepaute) is on display in Grand Haven's Train Depot Museum. Unresolved. 5) Material and height: Conservancy '52-foot steel tower'; NPS 51 ft cast iron; USLHS 52 ft height above mean high water, cast iron. Story says cast iron per NPS and USLHS. 6) Keepers: the roster is the USLHS roster for the whole pier range (97 lines, 1872-1969), matched to this record by roster.py at 0.26 km (name and position). It is not split by tower, and it was not checked against the NARA registers. Mary Miller (roster) and 'Mrs. Harry Miller' (LF's list for the whole station) are not confirmed to be one woman. 7) 1961 rescue: the two young men are private individuals and are not named. David E. Sparks is named only in his public role (Coast Guard crewman, 1962 medal, per LF) and as the roster's principal keeper in 1961. 8) Local Board report (fiscal 1895) is cited by scan page; printed pages not read; the fiscal label is from the corpus. 9) Bulletin 1916 is cited by PDF page; the printed page was not read. OCR reads 'Pierhoad' for Pierhead, so the story does not quote the name. The index entry (1918-1923) is clean and used for the illuminant change; the Bulletin 1918 entry is OCR-garbled. 10) Lighthouse Friends is all-rights-reserved: used for facts only, with prose written here; quotes are short phrases kept for evidence checks. LF is the only source for the 1875, 1883/1885, 1886, 1889, 1906 and 1961 accounts. 11) The 1852 collapse concerns the first beach light, not this tower, and the story says so. 12) The record's characteristic (Oc R 4s) and range (5.2 nm) were not verified by a source read here and are left as recorded. 13) The 2026 tours of the outer light (Spectrum News, read in the sibling story) were not checked here, so the story makes no claim about 2026 tours. 14) Page reads: about 13 (LF cached, NPS archived, Conservancy, USLHS place, cyberlights, Board and Bulletin pages via corpus), plus 1 WebSearch and 1 newspaper search (no usable newspaper hit).
